question.text: Scenario: Ms. Prerna Desai, aged 28, is a software engineer earning Rs. 15 lakh per annum. She has the following financial goals: 1. Emergency fund: 6 months' expenses (monthly expenses Rs. 40,000) — needed immediately 2. Down payment for a house: Rs. 15 lakh in 3 years 3. Child's education fund: Rs. 50 lakh in 20 years 4. Retirement corpus: Rs. 5 crore in 32 years (retire at 60) She can save Rs. 50,000 per month. She is filing under the old tax regime and has not utilized her Section 80C limit. Her investment adviser, Mr. Kartik, suggests the following allocation: - Emergency fund: Rs. 2.4 lakh lump sum in a Liquid Fund (current yield ~6.5% p.a.) - House down payment: Rs. 30,000/month SIP in a Short Duration Debt Fund (expected return 7.5% p.a.) - Education fund: Rs. 10,000/month SIP in a Flexi-Cap Equity Fund (expected return 12% p.a., expense ratio 0.8% Direct Plan) - Retirement: Rs. 10,000/month SIP split between ELSS Fund (Rs. 5,000 for Section 80C) and Nifty 50 Index Fund (Rs. 5,000, expense ratio 0.15%) Total monthly SIP: Rs. 50,000. Prerna opts for Direct Plans and Growth option for all equity funds. Question 1 of 5: If Prerna invests Rs. 30,000/month via SIP in a Short Duration Debt Fund for 3 years at 7.5% p.a. return (compounded monthly), what is the approximate corpus she will accumulate for the house down payment? (Use FV of ordinary monthly annuity formula)

explanation.text: The Logic: FV of ordinary monthly annuity = PMT x [(1+r)^n - 1] / r, where PMT = Rs. 30,000, r = 0.075/12 = 0.00625 per month, and n = 36 months. FV = 30,000 x [(1.00625)^36 - 1] / 0.00625, which works out to approximately Rs. 12.07 lakh. Rounded to the nearest option, this is closest to Rs. 12.10 lakh. The Trap: Rs. 11.98 lakh appears close but is below the computed Rs. 12.07 lakh; the nearer option is Rs. 12.10 lakh. Note: Short-duration debt instruments are commonly used for short-horizon goals to match duration with the time to the goal.
